chapter: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
title: A lynching near Columbia, Missouri shatters him
summary: In his senior year in Columbia, Missouri, he heard of a lynching about 30 miles away, which frightened him and made him mature.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I was just trying to think of some more things in this town of Columbia, Missouri, because it was during this period that I really had -- excuse me. I presume one of the most influential incidents that happened, that was distasteful, that had something to do with my moving to another area, and that was -- and I hate to mention it but I think this is very significant, as you heard me say before during my conversation with you.

I would have to be completely dishonest not to mention these things and not to say that they didn't have something to do with my life. And during the time that I was finishing my high school education in Columbia, Missouri, where we moved, as

I said, after having lived in at least a dozen different cities which I've named some of them. I don't know all of them; Youngstown, Ohio, Columbus, Ohio, whatever, et cetera. During -- it was during my senior year, I was about to start my senior year for graduation of high school. In this environment in Columbia, Missouri, which was -- I didn't realize at the time about racial prejudices and violence at the time, because my interest was all in music and learning my schooling and having fun with the boys as a young fellow. And I wasn't aware of it although I think every black person was aware that the majority of white people in the south and the midwestern states in particular were not too fond to have black people around.

With the signs that they had, white and colored fountains and white and colored toilets, and as I said I would have had to be a complete idiot not to recognize this as a great handicap. And I never will forget it. During this period I heard about a lynching that they had about 30 miles from town, which means like 30 miles is the outskirts of town, as far as I'm concerned. You know yourself that 20 or 30 miles in any direction from your home is only -- it could be actually in the city limits.
And this not only frightened me, but it completely made me a mature man in my mind, because I

realized that this had happened and in my fear I also realized that I had to be a man in order to protect myself. And I realized that it would be almost impossible for me to further my education under these conditions, having had the background and training that I had had, and at that time I had never been that close to any racial conflict or violence. Where actually I would know about it, where it would affect me that much.
